title: The Cold Orbit
premise: Tamsin Sandoval has spent eleven years alone tending the Svalbard-adjacent seed vault and its mysterious beacon, a relic of a war that froze the world into two hostile orbital blocs. When the research ship Meridian returns from deep space with its crew biologically reversed to childhood, carrying a message encoded in their own cells, Tamsin learns the beacon was built by his missing mother as a failsafe — and that both blocs will kill to control it. As hunters close in on the vault, Tamsin must decode the message through the children's fragmented memories of a future they already lived. In the end he broadcasts the truth about who started the war, sacrificing the vault and his anonymity, and sends the rejuvenated crew back up as living proof that the future can be rewritten.
about_author: Edmund Reyes is a former radio engineer who spent a decade maintaining remote Arctic listening stations before turning to fiction. He writes quiet, claustrophobic science fiction about people left behind by grand narratives.

chapters.title: The Man Who Winds the Clock
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. We meet him in his meticulous routine: cataloging seeds, calibrating a beacon whose purpose no one at Central Command can explain. A routine supply drone arrives with a terse notice: the vault is scheduled for decommission. Emotional beat: loneliness sharpened into dread — his invisible life is ending.

chapters.title: Something Falling, Not Burning
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Against protocol he tracks a reentry signature and finds the Meridian downed on the ice shelf, intact but wrong. The crew are children wearing adult-sized flight suits, alive, disoriented, calling each other by ranks they shouldn't remember. Emotional beat: awe curdling into fear as Tamsin realizes the ship was declared lost nine years ago.

chapters.title: Children of the Long Voyage
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Tamsin and Ilsa Voss, the ship's captain now aged eight. The children retain procedural memory and fragments of a mission they refuse to describe fully. Ilsa recognizes the vault's beacon frequency and says only: 'It's still singing.' Emotional beat: fragile trust forming between caretaker and impossible survivors.

chapters.title: The Message in the Marrow
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Medical scans reveal data encoded in the children's cellular structure — a compressed record planted before the Meridian ever launched. Tamsin realizes the beacon isn't a transmitter; it's a decoder, and his mother designed it. Emotional beat: grief and betrayal, as inheritance becomes literal.

chapters.title: Visitors
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Two bloc shuttles arrive at the vault under pretense of inspection; their escorts are not inspectors. Tamsin hides the children in the deep cold archive while stalling the officers, buying hours with bureaucratic theater. Emotional beat: the thrill and terror of finally mattering, of being seen.

chapters.title: What Mother Left Running
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV, with flashbacks from her adult life aboard the Meridian. Through the decoding beacon, the first fragment resolves: the war's opening strike was falsified by a third party inside one bloc's command. Ilsa remembers choosing this mission knowing she'd come back a child. Emotional beat: loyalty tested against truth she swore to bury.

chapters.title: The Cold Between Stars
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The shuttles return with force; the vault's defenses fail section by section. One child, Pilot Anselm, is taken. Tamsin must choose: flee with the decoded half-message or stay and lose everything. He stays. Emotional beat: guilt, and the first deliberate act of courage in his small life.

chapters.title: Broadcast Rights
chapters.summary: Dual POV climax begins. From an ice-buried relay tower, Tamsin and Ilsa assemble the full message while bloc warships maneuver overhead, each side believing the other holds the vault. The final fragment names the falsifier — a hero revered by both sides. Emotional beat: terrible clarity; the truth cannot be owned, only told.

chapters.title: The Beacon Speaks
chapters.summary: Climax. Tamsin transmits the raw record on every open channel, unencrypted, unattributable, unstoppable. Both blocs' fleets hold fire as the evidence spreads through crews who were children once themselves. The vault burns behind him. Emotional beat: catharsis — the invisible man makes the loudest broadcast in human history.

chapters.title: Seeds for the Thaw
chapters.summary: Resolution, Tamsin's POV. Months later, ceasefire talks proceed shakily; the rejuvenated crew, led by eight-year-old Captain Voss, testify as living archives. Tamsin, no longer caretaker of anything, plants the salvaged seed collection in thawing ground near the ruins. Emotional beat: quiet hope — inheritance passed forward, memory made soil.
